 National foreword
 This document is part of the series of Eurocodes. Eurocodes have reference numbers from EN 1990 to EN 1999 and are regarded as a consistant set of design rules. Eurocodes assume the use of a number of parameters to be determined nationally, denoted Nationally Determined Parameters (NDP), given in a corresponding National Annex (NA). Eurocodes can only be used for the design of structures together with the NDPs applicable in the country where a structure or product is to be used.
 Therefore, this document can only be used as a basis for design of structures or products to be used in Norway together with the NDPs given in the Norwegian NA. This document specifies recommended values for the NDPs, but these cannot be used as replacement for the NDPs.
 NAs are in principle informative. According to § 10-2 of the Technical Regulations to The Planning and Building Act (pbl), it may be assumed that the requirements in The Planning and Building Act and the Technical Regulations are met, provided that methods and execution are in accordance with Norwegian Standard. Use of Eurocodes assumes that the corresponding NA, with the NDPs, is used as basis for the design. Consequently, the NAs shall be considered as normative.
 Information on the Eurocodes is found on www.eurokoder.no.

(1) EN 1993-1-3 gives design requirements for cold-formed thin gauge members and sheeting. It applies to cold-formed steel products made from coated or uncoated thin gauge hot or cold rolled sheet or strip, that have been cold-formed by such processes as cold-rolled forming or press-braking. It may also be used for the design of profiled steel sheeting for composite steel and concrete slabs at the construction stage, see EN 1994. The execution of steel structures made of cold-formed thin gauge members and sheeting is covered in EN 1090.
 NOTE: The rules in this part complement the rules in other parts of EN 1993-1.
 (2) Methods are also given for stressed-skin design using steel sheeting as a structural diaphragm.
 (3) This part does not apply to cold-formed circular and rectangular structural hollow sections supplied to EN 10219, for which reference should be made to EN 1993-1-1 and EN 1993-1-8.
 (4) EN 1993-1-3 gives methods for design by calculation and for design assisted by testing. The methods for design by calculation apply only within stated ranges of material properties and geometrical proportions for which sufficient experience and test evidence is available. These limitations do not apply to design assisted by testing.
 (5) EN 1993-1-3 does not cover load arrangement for testing for loads during execution and maintenance.
 (6) The calculation rules given in this standard are only valid if the tolerances of the cold formed members comply with EN 1090-2

Supplementary to EN 1993-1-1, for the purposes of this Part 1-3 of EN 1993, the following terms and definitions apply:
 1.3.1
 The flat sheet steel material out of which cold-formed sections and profiled sheets are made by cold-forming.
 basic yield strength
 The tensile yield strength of the basic material.
 1.3.3
 Structural behaviour involving in-plane shear in the sheeting.
 1.3.4
 liner tray
 Profiled sheet with large lipped edge stiffeners, suitable for interlocking with adjacent liner trays to form a plane of ribbed sheeting that is capable of supporting a parallel plane of profiled sheeting spanning perpendicular to the span of the liner trays.
 1.3.5
 Restriction of the lateral or rotational movement, or the torsional or warping deformation, of a member or element, that increases its buckling resistance in a similar way to a spring support, but to a lesser extent than a rigid support.
 1.3.6
 relative slenderness
 A normalized non-dimensional slenderness ratio.
 1.3.7
 Restriction of the lateral or rotational movement, or the torsional or warping deformation, of a member or element, that increases its buckling resistance to the same extent as a rigid support.
 1.3.8
 A design method that allows for the contribution made by diaphragm action in the sheeting to the stiffness and strength of a structure.
 A location at which a member is able to transfer forces or moments to a foundation, or to another member or other structural component.
 A target average thickness inclusive zinc and other metallic coating layers when present rolled and defined by the steel supplier (tnom not including organic coatings).
 1.3.11
 A nominal thickness minus zinc and other metallic coating layers (tcor).
 the steel core thickness used in design by calculation according to 1.5.3(6) and 3.2.4.

The image is a page from the standard “EN 1993-1-3: 2006 (E)” showing a subsection titled **“1.5 Terminology and conventions for dimensions”** with a focus on **“1.5.1 Form of sections.”** The upper portion contains printed explanatory text, aligned left, describing cold-formed members and profiled sheets. It states that, within permitted tolerances, cold-formed members/profiled sheets have **constant nominal thickness along the entire length**, and may have either **uniform** or **tapering** cross-sections. It also notes that their cross-sections essentially comprise **plane elements connected by curved elements**, and that **typical section forms are shown in Figure 1.1**. There is also a note indicating that the calculation methods of this part do not cover all cases shown in the referenced figures.

Beneath the text, the page includes a diagram labeled **“Figure 1.1: Typical forms of sections for cold-formed members.”** The figure is divided into three labeled categories with schematic cross-sections drawn as thin black outline shapes. The shapes represent idealized metallic cross-sectional profiles (typically with straight and curved corners to show lips, flanges, webs, and bends typical of cold-formed steel).

### a) Single open sections (top group)
On the left-to-right upper row, multiple small cross-section sketches are shown under the caption **“a) Single open sections.”** These appear as individual profiles with one main open side, including variations resembling **C-like, Z-like, lipped channel forms, and forked/stepped edge profiles**. Some shapes include a protruding lip or curved transition at the free edges, suggesting **flanges with edge stiffening (lips)**. The cross-sections have both vertical/oblique plate elements and rounded corner radii where bends occur.

### b) Open built-up sections (middle group)
In the middle row group under **“b) Open built-up sections,”** the sketches show **composite/assembled open shapes**, typically resembling two separated plates or channels spaced apart, with a central web and protruding elements on one or both sides. These drawings suggest **built-up members** formed by combining plates or elements without forming a fully enclosed perimeter. The outlines include clearly defined corners and consistent bend radii.

### c) Closed built-up sections (bottom group)
At the bottom row under **“c) Closed built-up sections,”** there are two larger schematic profiles that appear as **fully enclosed rectangles/squares with thickness variations**—illustrating members where the perimeter forms a closed shape. The corners show curved bend radii, and the interior regions indicate an enclosed cavity, consistent with **closed hollow or boxed built-up profiles**.

Overall, the figure uses a clean, monochrome schematic style (thin line art) to convey typical cold-formed cross-section typologies (single open, open built-up, and closed built-up), emphasizing the geometry of plate elements joined by curved bends, which aligns with the surrounding textual definitions about cross-section form.

The image is a technical diagram page showing examples of cold-formed steel cross-sections, labeled “Figure 1.2: Examples of cold-formed members and profiled sheets.” It is organized into three main subfigures (a), (b), and (c), each illustrating typical shapes relevant to compression/tension members, bending members, and profiled sheets/liner trays.

**Overall layout and axes:**  
Each cross-section drawing is presented in black linework with dashed reference lines indicating principal axes. At the center of many sections, circular markers and intersecting dashed horizontal/vertical lines denote the main axis location(s). The figure uses consistent styling (thin black outlines with gray dashed construction lines) to emphasize geometric form rather than dimensions.

**(a) Compression members and tension members:**  
Across the top portion, multiple isolated cross-sections are shown (single open, open built-up, and closed built-up forms). Examples include:  
- Single open “channel-like” or “C”-type shapes and thicker variants resembling lipped channels.  
- Cross-sections resembling “I” or “H”/built-up forms made from multiple plates or walls joined together.  
- A clearly closed rectangular or box-like section variant, drawn as a full outline with internal dashed centerlines.  
- A star/plus-like built-up form with multiple flanges meeting around a central region (an X/cross arrangement).  
These shapes demonstrate that cold-formed members may be open or closed and may consist of several plane elements joined by curved edges.

**(b) Beams and other members subject to bending:**  
The middle portion shows a set of bending-oriented cross-sections, mostly “I/” “T/” and “Z/” like forms and lipped variants. The drawings include:  
- Multiple “C/U” or “Z” shaped lipped channels with asymmetry in the flange lips.  
- “X”-like or hourglass-like double-web configurations indicating members with two opposing thin walls.  
- A sequence of progressively different geometric profiles (including those with varying flange lengths and lip positions), again with dashed axis lines through the center.  
This section visually supports the idea that main bending properties depend on where the principal axes lie, which may be defined by symmetry or imposed by connecting members.

**(c) Profiled sheets and liner trays:**  
The bottom portion shows wave/trapezoidal profiles typical of profiled sheet decking or liner trays. Several series of repeated corrugations are displayed:  
- Multiple-row repeating trapezoid patterns with different heights and spacing, drawn as continuous outlines.  
- Ribbed/wave forms with alternating crest and trough geometries.  
- A few flat-to-lipped tray-like profiles with side boundaries that fold upward slightly, representing liner tray edges.  

**Textual captioning:**  
At the bottom, the caption “(c) Profiled sheets and liner trays” and the overall figure caption confirm the purpose: examples of cold-formed members and profiled sheets used in structural applications, consistent with the provided context about plane elements joined by curved elements, constant nominal thickness within tolerances, and common section families.

 (2) The cross-sections of cold-formed members and profiled sheets essentially comprise a number of plane elements joined by curved elements.
 (3) Typical forms of sections for cold-formed members are shown in figure 1.1.

The image appears to be a cropped textbook-style diagram (Figure 1.3) illustrating “Typical forms of stiffeners for cold-formed members and sheeting.” The background is white with black line drawings and minimal labels. Near the bottom, the caption text reads: “Figure 1.3: Typical forms of stiffeners for cold-formed members and sheeting.”

Three stiffener concepts are visible, each shown as simple cross-sectional linework (thick black outlines with slender internal lines used for bends or voids). The left side contains part of option (a) while the right side contains the full (b) and (c) along with partial additional markings at the top.

**(a) Folds and bends**: On the left, there are several short, rectilinear and angled shapes representing stiffener geometries created by forming folds or bends in sheet or member walls. The shapes are drawn as straight segments connected by sharp corners, suggesting multiple fold patterns. Some elements resemble protrusions or re-entrant bends along a plate surface. Only part of the option is visible, but it clearly categorizes stiffeners created through bending rather than adding separate components.

**(b) Folded groove and curved groove**: On the upper right, option (b) shows a horizontal plate line (top and bottom edges) with a middle groove formed by a V- or U-like depression. The groove has a rounded/curved central region with symmetric side walls sloping inward toward the middle. The ends of the plate remain straight, while the central groove creates local stiffness by increasing section depth through forming.

**(c) Bolted angle stiffener**: Below (b), option (c) depicts an angle stiffener attached by a bolt. A horizontal member line is shown, with a vertical short segment downward from its underside forming an “L” or right-angle geometry (angle section). A small bolt symbol (or fastener indicator) is centered at the connection point, where a short line extends downward and a dashed or slender vertical alignment line indicates the fastening location. The drawing implies a stiffener made from an angle section that is mechanically fastened rather than formed as a single sheet bend.

Overall, the image uses simplified geometric cross-sections to compare how cold-formed stiffeners can be produced either by **integral forming** (folds, bends, grooves) or by **external attachment** (bolted angle stiffener), consistent with the surrounding context about longitudinal flange stiffeners including edge and intermediate types.

The image is a cropped figure from a technical document. It contains monochrome vector diagrams showing cross-sectional stiffener shapes along sheet or panel edges, likely for cold-formed steel members. The background is white, with black line drawings representing the stiffener geometry. The crop includes two partial schematic panels at the top, suggesting multiple sub-figures (labeled letters) within the same figure.

On the left, one schematic shows a short edge stiffener profile: a vertical or near-vertical line at the left end connects to a horizontal segment, with a right-angle corner indicating a fold at the edge. The linework is thick and uniform, typical of engineering diagrams. The visible portion suggests a “single” edge fold configuration where the sheet edge is bent once to create a stiffening flange.

**Table 5.1 (EN 1993-1-3): Maximum width-to-thickness ratios for design by calculation (Part 1-3)**

This table defines **limits on element slenderness** for which the **design-by-calculation provisions** in the relevant part of EN 1993 may be applied. It sets **maximum allowable ratios of widths to thicknesses** for different cross-section elements, using the notation **b, c, d, h, t**, as indicated in the accompanying EN figure/table conventions (b, c and d are widths of particular elements; h is a overall element height; t is the thickness; and φ is an angle for sloped elements).

The table has two columns:
1. **“Element of cross-section”** – identifies the type of plated/formed element (e.g., vertical web element, channel with a lip, lipped channel, built-up shapes, and sloped elements) through small schematic drawings.
2. **“Maximum value”** – provides the corresponding **upper bounds** expressed as **ratio limits** (e.g., **b/t ≤ 50**) and, where relevant, additional limits for lip dimensions such as **c/t** and **d/t**.

### Rows / element types and ratio limits

1. **Web-like vertical element (singe element with width b)**  
   - Limit: **b/t ≤ 50**  
   This row applies to an element whose effective width participating in the width-to-thickness check is represented by **b**.

2. **Channel/flange with a lip dimension c (single lip case)**  
   - Limits:  
     - **b/t ≤ 60**  
     - **c/t ≤ 50**  
   Here, **b** is the overall relevant width for the flange/channel element, while **c** is the **lip projection width**, measured **perpendicular to the flange** when the lip is not perpendicular (per Table notes context).

3. **Lipped element with both c and d dimensions (two-direction lip/return case)**  
   - Limits:  
     - **b/t ≤ 90**  
     - **c/t ≤ 60**  
     - **d/t ≤ 50**  
   The presence of **both lip measures** indicates that the element has additional folded features: **c** (one lip/return) and **d** (the other return or distance as defined in EN 1993-1-3 for that geometry).

4. **Outer vertical element of a section with wide b (larger plate width case)**  
   - Limit: **b/t ≤ 500**  
   This permissive value indicates a geometry where the controlling instability/slenderness mechanism is less severe (relative to the other cases), and the governing criterion becomes far less restrictive for the stated element.

5. **Sloped or angled element (inclined plate with angle φ; height h)**  
   - Limits: **45° ≤ φ ≤ 90°**  
   - And: **h/t ≤ 500 sin φ**  
   This row governs **inclined elements**; the allowable slenderness depends on the slope via **sin φ**. The table explicitly restricts φ to **between 45° and 90°**.

### Important interpretation notes (from the provided context)
- The ratio limits in Table 5.1 **define the range of applicability** for using the **design-by-calculation provisions**. Outside these limits, the designer should not rely on the stated calculation rules unless the cross-section is **verified** via **testing and/or calculations confirmed by an appropriate number of tests**.
- If **c/b < 0.2** or **d/b < 0.1**, then the **lip should be ignored**, effectively taking **c = 0 or d = 0** for the purposes of the checks.
- These limits **do not apply** when **effective cross-section properties are determined by testing and by calculations** (i.e., experimental verification regimes).
- The definition of **c** is perpendicular to the flange when the lip is not perpendicular to it.

Overall, Table 5.1 is a **geometry-dependent slenderness gate**: it maps each schematic cross-section element type to a set of **maximum width-to-thickness ratios** that must be satisfied for EN 1993 Part 1-3 calculation methods to be applicable.

It is arranged as a sequence of sub-figures **a) through f)** showing how an intermediate stiffener’s effective cross-section is determined and then refined using distortional buckling (flexural buckling of the intermediate stiffener) and optional iteration.

**Common elements across the diagrams:**
- The stiffener is depicted as a **thick dark horizontal element** in the middle with **thin hatched plane elements** to the left and right (representing adjacent plane elements with effective widths).
- **Support triangles** are drawn at the boundaries, indicating spring/continuity restraint conditions (shown by different “K” or “K=∞” assumptions).
- **Arrows and labels** indicate stresses/ratios such as **\(f_{yb}/\gamma_{M0}\)** and the elastic critical buckling stress **\(\sigma_{cr,s}\)**.
- The **stiffener thickness** is shown as **\(t\)**, sometimes reduced to **\(t_{red}\)** in later steps.
- The effective widths are labeled **\(b_{1,e1}\), \(b_{1,e2}\), \(b_{2,e1}\), \(b_{2,e2}\)** and the additional stiffener width **\(b_s\)** (represented in the central element).
- A centroid reference **axis \(a-a\)** is shown around the stiffener line where effective second moment of area would be taken.

**Sub-figure a) “Gross cross-section and boundary conditions”:**
- Shows a composite cross-section with the stiffener between adjacent plane regions.
- Plane elements are hatched; boundary/support conditions are indicated with triangular supports on both sides.
- The effective widths are annotated (left and right), including two sub-indices per side suggesting different effective portions.
- The vertical distance dimension marks thickness **\(t\)** and indicates where buckling restraint is considered.

**Sub-figure b) “Step 1: Effective cross-section for K = ∞”:**
- Depicts the top hatched plane elements expanded by arrows labeled with effective widths **\(b_{1,e2}\)** and **\(b_{2,e2}\)** (and related terms).
- A curved/zigzag symbol and a large spring restraint indicator show **full restraint** (since **K = ∞**).
- The assumed uniform compressive stress is indicated as **\(\sigma_{com,Ed} = f_{yb}/\gamma_{M0}\)**.

**Sub-figure c) “Step 2: Elastic critical stress \(\sigma_{cr,s}\) for effective area \(A_s\)”:**
- The stiffener is shown with **“a–a”** and central axis; a symbol resembling a buckling mode shape appears (V-shaped/undulating deflection).
- The label **\(\sigma_{cr,s}\)** appears near the buckled shape, with side supports.

**Sub-figure d) “Reduced strength \(\chi_d f_{yb}/\gamma_{M0}\) … with reduction factor \(\chi_d\)”**:
- Shows the buckled mode again but now with the strength reduced: text indicates **\(\chi_d f_{yb}/\gamma_{M0}\)**.
- “Iteration 1” is annotated on the left, implying an iterative refinement process.

**Sub-figures e) “Step 3: Optionally repeat step 1 with reduced compressive stress”**:
- Shows “Iteration n” with an updated effective width calculation.
- The compressive stress driving the recalculation is indicated as **\(\chi_d f_{yb}/\gamma_{M0}\)**, and the iteration continues until **\(\chi_{d,n} \approx \chi_{d,(n-1)}\)**.

**Sub-figure f) “Adopt an effective cross-section with reduced thickness \(t_{red}\)”**:
- Displays the final effective cross-section concept with reduced thickness marked **\(t_{red}\)** in the stiffener region (and implicitly correspondingly for the included elements).
- Effective widths are now labeled generically as **\(b_{1,e2,n}\)** and **\(b_{2,e1,n}\)** (showing the iterated results for each side).
- The central buckling-restrained depiction remains, indicating that the reduced effective cross-section is used for subsequent resistance calculations.

Overall, the figure provides a step-by-step visual algorithm: start with full restraint (**K=∞**) to determine effective widths and area of the intermediate stiffener, compute an elastic critical buckling stress, convert that into a distortional buckling reduction factor **\(\chi_d\)**, optionally iterate by recalculating effective widths with reduced compressive stress, and finally implement the result by reducing the effective thickness to **\(t_{red}\)** for use in effective section properties.

The table excerpt provides **acceptance limits and parameter definitions** used to determine the **local transverse resistance per web** of an unstiffened web in cross-sections with two or more webs (including sheeting), as referenced in equations (6.18)–(6.20). It is structured as a set of **inequality-based criteria** and **category-dependent rules** for an **effective bearing length** \(l_a\), which then feeds the resistance calculation.

## 1) Section eligibility / geometric limits (items (6.17a)–(6.17c))
The table lists three inequality checks that must be satisfied for the method to apply:

- **(6.17a)**: \(\; r/t \le 10\)  
  *Meaning:* the **corner internal radius \(r\)** relative to **web thickness \(t\)** must not be excessive.

- **(6.17b)**: \(\; h_w/t \le 200\sin\varphi\)  
  *Meaning:* the **web height between flange midlines \(h_w\)** compared to **thickness \(t\)** is limited by an expression involving the **web inclination angle \(\varphi\)**.

- **(6.17c)**: \(\; 45^\circ \le \varphi \le 90^\circ\)  
  *Meaning:* the web angle relative to the flanges is restricted to moderately to steep orientations.

These criteria determine whether the cross-section geometry falls within the calibrated range for calculating local transverse resistance.

## 2) Category selection based on clear distances (from figure 6.9 context)
Although the table is partially text-extracted, it clearly indicates **two categories** for applying the effective bearing length \(l_a\), depending on the **clear distance** between:
- the **local load** and the **nearest support** (\(e\)), or
- the **support reaction or local load** and a **free end** (\(c\)).

The rules shown imply:
- **Category 1** applies when the relevant clear distance satisfies **\(e \le 1.5 h_w\)** or **\(c \le 1.5 h_w\)**.
- **Category 2** applies when **\(e > 1.5 h_w\)** or **\(c > 1.5 h_w\)**.
- Additional subcases include whether the support is at an **end support** or an **internal support**.

## 3) Effective bearing length \(l_a\) rules (equations (6.19a)–(6.19c))
For each category, the table gives piecewise values of \(l_a\):

### Category 1
- **(6.19a)**: \(l_a = 10\,\text{mm}\)

### Category 2 (dependence on \(\beta_V\) and interpolation)
For Category 2, \(l_a\) is governed by a parameter \(\beta_V\):

- If **\(-\beta_V \le 0.2\)**:  
  \[
  l_a = \, s_s
  \]
- If **\(\beta_V \ge 0.3\)**:  
  \[
  l_a = 10\,\text{mm}
  \]
- If **\(0.2 < -\beta_V < 0.3\)** (shown as a transition region with linear interpolation):  
  \(l_a\) is obtained by **linear interpolation** between the two limiting values above.

The table also references a profile-specific interpolation parameter \(a\) (equations (6.20a)–(6.20d)) for sheeting profiles versus liner trays and hat sections, and again separated by Category 1 vs Category 2—used to compute coefficients for the resistance formula.

## Overall meaning for RAG indexing
This table functions as a **gatekeeper and parameter-selection guide**: first, it establishes **geometric applicability limits** \((r/t,\; h_w/t,\; \varphi)\); then it instructs how to choose **Category 1/2** using **\(e\) or \(c\)** relative to \(1.5h_w\); finally it specifies the **piecewise effective bearing length** \(l_a\), including a \(\beta_V\)-dependent interpolation.

The image is a technical textbook page (EN 1993-1-3: 2006, Figure 6.9) containing schematic cross-sections and diagrams used to define “categories” for local transverse resistance of unstiffened webs in cold-formed/cross-section members with two or more webs. The page is vertically divided into multiple stacked panels, each showing a simplified cross-section of a member with side supports (represented by vertical lines/blocks) and a web height dimension labeled \(h_w\). Local load or support reaction is shown as a cluster of short arrows (downward or upward) near a location on the member.

Each panel includes specific horizontal clear distances from the load/reaction to either the nearest support or a free end:
- \(e\): clear distance from the local load to the nearest support (used for Category 1/2 depending on whether \(e \le 1.5h_w\) or \(e > 1.5h_w\)).
- \(c\): clear distance from the bearing length for the support reaction or local load to a free end (used for Category 1/2 depending on whether \(c \le 1.5h_w\) or \(c > 1.5h_w\)).
- \(s_s\): an additional short spacing dimension near the bearing/load zone, drawn with double-headed arrows above the local load arrows (repeated across panels).  

The diagrams show different support/load arrangements:
1) Top panel: local load applied between supports. The load arrow cluster is drawn near the top chord/plate region, with \(e\) measured from the load to the nearest support. A label indicates “Category 1 – local load applied with \(e \le 1,5 h_w\) clear from the nearest support.”
2) Second panel: local load near a free end, with \(c\) measured to the free end. Labeled “Category 1 – local load applied with \(c \le 1,5 h_w\) clear from a free end.”
3) Third panel: reaction at an end support, with \(c\) to the free end. Labeled “Category 1 – reaction at end support with \(c \le 1,5 h_w\) clear from a free end.”
4) Fourth panel (start of Category 2 group): local load between supports but farther away, with \(e\) shown and the label “Category 2 – local load applied with \(e > 1,5 h_w\) clear from the nearest support.”
5) Fifth panel: local load near a free end with larger \(c\); label “Category 2 – local load applied with \(c > 1,5 h_w\) clear from a free end.”
6) Sixth panel: reaction at an end support with larger \(c\); label “Category 2 – reaction at end support with \(c > 1,5 h_w\) clear from a free end.”
7) Seventh (bottom) panel within the Category 2 group: “reaction at internal support,” with a reaction arrow cluster upward at an internal support location. Only \(h_w\) is emphasized for the internal support configuration, and \(s_s\) is shown near the reaction bearing zone.

Overall, the figure provides a visual rule-set for classifying the cross-section category based on the relative distance of the bearing (load or reaction) to the nearest support or free edge, using thresholds tied to \(1.5h_w\).

**Table 6.3 – Appropriate buckling curve for various cross-sections (torsional / torsional-flexural buckling context)**

This table provides guidance for selecting the *buckling curve* to be used in design when evaluating the *buckling resistance* of compression members subject to instability modes that involve **torsion** and/or **torsional-flexural interaction**, rather than purely flexural buckling. In the surrounding design checks (as indicated by the accompanying text), the designer first determines the relevant elastic critical forces (e.g., \(N_{cr,T}\) for torsional buckling and \(N_{cr,TF}\) for torsional-flexural buckling) and then derives the design buckling resistance \(N_{b,Rd}\) from **EN 1993-1-1, 6.3.1.1**, using an appropriate **buckling curve for buckling about the z–z axis** taken from this table (see notes (4)).

### Structure and meaning
- The **primary column** lists the **Type of cross-section** (illustrated schematically). Each schematic corresponds to a common open section family and indicates how the section’s symmetry/asymmetry affects the governing buckling mode(s).
- Adjacent text fragments (partly visible on the right side) indicate conditional selection based on whether certain symmetry-related geometric properties hold, e.g.:
  - conditions involving \(f_{yb}\) and \(f_{ya}\) (typical of EN 1993 curve usage, where the choice between lower/upper imperfection factors or curve types depends on whether the applicable buckling mode is governed by one or the other principal direction).
- The table’s intent is therefore: **map the cross-section geometry to the correct buckling curve designation(s)** to be used in the calculation of buckling resistance for the governing instability mode.

### Cross-section families shown (schematic categories)
The table includes multiple schematic illustrations, consistent with the EN 1993 treatment of open sections, including:
1. **Point-symmetric open sections** (example context: Z-purlin with equal flanges). For such sections, the table context emphasizes that the **torsional buckling resistance may be lower than flexural buckling resistance**. Therefore, torsional/torsional-flexural buckling can govern.
2. **Mono-symmetric open sections** (explicitly referenced in the context, with “see figure 6.12”). Here the table supports the possibility that **torsional-flexural buckling resistance may be less than flexural buckling resistance**, so the chosen buckling curve must reflect torsional-flexural behavior.
3. **Non-symmetric open sections** (“other cross-section”), where torsional and/or torsional-flexural buckling may be weaker than flexural buckling, requiring selection of the correct buckling curve that corresponds to the governing instability pattern.

### Connection to the preceding design steps
The table should be used after:
- determining which mode governs (flexural vs torsional vs torsional-flexural) based on the elastic critical forces (notes (5)–(7));
- then selecting the **relevant buckling curve** for the **z–z axis** as required by EN 1993-1-1 (note (4)).

### Important technical dependencies highlighted by the context
- The notes emphasize that for torsional-flexural buckling, the elastic critical force depends on section symmetry parameters (e.g., shear centre coordinates such as \(y_0, z_0\)) and must satisfy conditions such as comparison with \(N_{cr,y}\) and \(N_{cr,z}\) (see note (6)).
- The appropriate buckling curve in Table 6.3 is thus not a generic “one-size-fits-all” selection; it is tied to **which buckling mode is critical** and therefore indirectly to **the section symmetry class shown by the table**.

**In summary:** Table 6.3 is a lookup table that assigns the correct EN 1993 buckling curve (for buckling about the z–z axis) to the *type of open cross-section*, using schematic categorization and conditional criteria. Its purpose is to ensure that, when torsional or torsional-flexural buckling may govern (especially for mono-symmetric and non-symmetric open sections, and potentially for point-symmetric ones), the design buckling resistance uses the appropriate imperfection/buckling curve rather than one based only on flexural behavior.

Overall, the figure illustrates how the **location of fasteners within the corrugated trough geometry** affects the **design pull-through resistance**, presented with clear factor multipliers on arrows for three cases: central, quarter-point, and both quarter-points.

**Table 8.1 Description – Design resistances for blind rivets (EN 1993-1-8 context)**

This table provides **design resistance values** for **mechanical fasteners of the type blind rivet**, focusing on the resistance mechanisms relevant for structural design under static loading. It is used to derive the **design shear resistance** and **design tension resistance** (and, by implication, the related pull-through resistance where applicable) using parameters defined elsewhere in EN 1993-1-8.

At the top of the table, the text indicates a governing limit relation for the **pull-through resistance** under certain conditions. A key expression shown is of the form:

- **\(F_{b,Rd} \le f_{u1} e_1 t / (1.2 \gamma_{M2})\)**  
  (the snippet shows a bound involving **\(f_{u1}\)**, **\(e_1\)**, **\(t\)**, and the factor **\(\gamma_{M2}\)**).

The table then defines a **geometric reduction / interpolation parameter \(\alpha\)**, with a piecewise definition:

- **\(\alpha = 3.6 \sqrt{t/d}\)** for **\(\alpha \le 2.1\)**, but also explicitly states an upper/lower treatment:
  - **\(\alpha \le 2.1\)**, with **\(\alpha = 2.1\)** as a cap in the shown region.
  - It also states that intermediate values of **\(\alpha\)** are obtained by **linear interpolation**.

The table includes an explicit note that, for some resistances, values may be **determined by testing** (marked with a superscript “1)” in the document context). In particular, it indicates:
- **\(F_{v,Rd} = F_{v,Rk} / \gamma_{M2}\)** (conversion from characteristic to design resistance using the partial factor).

It further includes conditions for the applicability of the resistance formulas and references a relationship for design shear resistance depending on a **reduction factor for long joints**, denoted **\(\beta L_f\)**, with text resembling:
- **\(F_{b,Rd} / (n \beta L_f)\)** or an alternative minimum requirement such as  
  **\(F_{v,Rd} \ge 1.2 F_{n?} F_{t?}\)** (the snippet is partially truncated, but clearly the table provides inequality-based verification conditions between shear and pull-through mechanisms, often using multipliers like 1.2).

Rows/sections also highlight that **pull-through resistance \(F_{p,Rd}\)** is **to be determined by testing** in the shown cases (again marked with superscript “1)”), and that some resistance types (e.g., **pull-through in tension**) are not covered beyond certain validity ranges without experimental data.

Finally, the table contains **ranges of validity** for the fastener geometry, e.g.:
- A stated **rivet diameter range**: **\(2.6 \text{ mm} \le d \le 6.4 \text{ mm}\)**.
- A statement defining **sheet location/geometry**: e.g., the **thinnest sheet is next to the preformed head** of the blind rivet.
- A statement indicating that **cartridge fired pins may be used beyond ranges** only if resistance is determined from tests (present in the surrounding excerpt; for Table 8.1 the relevant meaning is that blind rivet validity is limited unless test evidence is available).

**Overall purpose for RAG retrieval:** Table 8.1 consolidates EN 1993-1-8 design rules for **blind rivets** by (a) defining geometric factors (notably **\(\alpha\)**), (b) providing formulas to compute **design resistance** from characteristic resistance using **\(\gamma_{M2}\)**, (c) setting **piecewise limits and interpolation rules**, and (d) specifying **when testing is required** and the **validity ranges** for rivet diameter and connection configuration.

**Table 8.2: Design resistances for self-tapping screws (EN 1993-1-8 context, partial factors applied)**

This table provides design formulae for the **resistances of mechanical fasteners that are self-tapping screws** under predominantly static loading. It expresses characteristic mechanical failure modes as **design resistances** using the **partial factor for materials/fasteners**.

---

### 1) Design resistance factors and variables (global context)
The table uses a **resistance reduction/partial factor** written as **\(\gamma_{M2}\)** (recommended value **1.25**, possibly overridden by the National Annex). The design resistances in the table are multiplied or divided consistently so that **\(\gamma_{M2}\)** appears in each expression.

Key geometric/material variables referenced in the table include:
- \(A\), **\(A_{net}\)**: gross area of fastener / tensile stress area / net cross-sectional area of the connected part (the table’s formulas use \(A_{net}\)).
- \(d\): **nominal screw diameter** (often related to hole diameter criteria, but the table itself focuses on resistance).
- \(d_w\): **washer/head diameter** (used for pull-through).
- \(t\), \(t_{1}\): thicknesses of connected sheets (used in edge and pull-through-related expressions).
- \(t_{sup}\): thickness of the supporting member in which the screw is fixed.
- \(f_u\): ultimate tensile strength (used with \(A_{net}\)).
- \(f_{u,sup}\): ultimate tensile strength of supporting material for pull-through/pull-out-type modes.
- \(s\): **thread pitch** (used in the choice between two pull-through resistance coefficients).
- \(p_1, p_2\): spacings of fasteners center-to-center (used indirectly through validity limits and the long-joint reduction factor \(\beta L_f\) according to EN 1993-1-8; the table shows conditions involving \(p_1\)).
- \(\alpha\): an exponent/parameter defined by formula depending on thickness-to-diameter ratio (used to compute a shear/tension-related coefficient).

---

### 2) Main resistance modes covered
The table distinguishes several relevant resistance mechanisms:

#### (a) Tensile resistance (pull-through/tension capacity in the connected part)
A tensile design resistance is given as:
\[
F_{n,Rd} = A_{net}\, f_u \,/\, \gamma_{M2}
\]
(i.e., the connected part’s net tensile stress area multiplied by ultimate tensile strength, with \(\gamma_{M2}\) as the design factor.)

#### (b) Shear resistance
The **shear resistance** \(F_{v,Rd}\) is stated as either:
- determined by testing (footnote indicates testing may be required), or
- calculated by a reduction using \(\gamma_{M2}\) and a factor \(F_{v,Rk}\):
\[
F_{v,Rd} = F_{v,Rk}/\gamma_{M2}
\]
The table also includes a **combined-shear regularity criterion** (a requirement comparing the sum of shear resistances to a multiple of an individual shear resistance):
\[
\sum F_{v,Rd} \ge 1.2\,F_{b,Rd}
\quad \text{or} \quad
\sum F_{v,Rd} \ge 1.2\,F_{v,Rd}
\]
(Displayed in the image as two alternative statements; the intent is to ensure shear distribution/compatibility across multiple screws.)

#### (c) Pull-through resistance
The table gives **pull-through resistance** \(F_{p,Rd}\) based on washer/head diameter:
\[
F_{p,Rd} = d_w\, t\, f_u \,/\, \gamma_{M2}
\]
It also provides a **supporting-member pull-out/pull-through resistance** \(F_{o,Rd}\) with different coefficients depending on the ratio \(s/t\) (thread pitch criterion), expressed as:
- for \(s/t < 1\):
\[
F_{o,Rd} = 0.45\, d\, t_{sup}\, f_{u,sup}/\gamma_{M2}
\]
- for \(s/t \ge 1\):
\[
F_{o,Rd} = 0.65\, d\, t_{sup}\, f_{u,sup}/\gamma_{M2}
\]

A further statement indicates that the governing tension/pull-through-type capacity should satisfy a minimum comparison, such as:
\[
\sum F_{p,Rd} \text{ or } F_{t,Rd} \ge F_{o,Rd}
\]
meaning the design resistance considering different failure modes must not be lower than the controlling pull-through-type mechanism.

---

### 3) Definition and use of \(\alpha\)
The table contains an expression for \(\alpha\) as a function of \(\sqrt{t/d}\) (with an upper cap at \(\alpha \le 2.1\)), with a piecewise or conditional definition depending on the thickness \(t\):
- \( \alpha = 3.2 \sqrt{t/d}\) with \(\alpha \le 2.1\)
- another branch shown with \(\alpha = 3.2 \sqrt[3]{t/d}\) / alternate scaling (the image shows two similar regimes, each capped)
- for larger values of the ratio or thickness, \(\alpha\) is taken as \(2.1\)
and **interpolation** is used in intermediate ranges to obtain \(\alpha\).

This \(\alpha\) is then used in the formula for a resistive coefficient such as:
\[
F_{b,Rd} = \alpha\, f_u\, d\, t \,/\, \gamma_{M2}
\]
(or an equivalent expression shown as \(\,F_{b,Rd} = \alpha f_u dt/\gamma_{M2}\), consistent with the visible structure).

---

### 4) Validity limits / geometry conditions shown
The bottom part of the table lists applicability conditions. The visible ones include:
- Longitudinal spacing criterion:
\[
p_1 \ge 3d,\quad \text{and a range for } d:\; 3.0\,\text{mm} \le d \le 8.0\,\text{mm}
\]
- A further spacing statement:
\[
p_2 \ge 3d
\]
- Thickness validity:
\[
t \le 1.5\,\text{mm},\quad t_1 \ge 0.9\,\text{mm}
\]
The table also states an installation condition such as: **the thinnest sheet is next to the head of the screw**, ensuring the assumed load transfer mechanism and local deformation pattern.

---

### 5) Footnotes / special notes included in the table
Footnotes reference:
- shear resistance may require **testing** for certain configurations,
- cartridge fired pins and other symbols are treated elsewhere (not applicable directly here, but the section numbering reflects broader fastener rules),
- additional National Annex information may be provided (especially for shear resistance and tension-related modes),
- deformation capacity requirements: if required and the conditions are not met, other structural parts must be proven to provide the needed deformation capacity.

---

**Overall**, Table 8.2 is a compact design-calculation table that supplies **closed-form design resistance expressions** for self-tapping screws—covering **tension**, **shear**, and **pull-through-type** mechanisms—while also specifying **piecewise coefficient rules**, **governing selection/inequality checks**, and **geometric validity limits** (spacing and thickness) under which the formulas are applicable.

**Table 8.3: Design resistances for cartridge fired pins (EN 1993-1-8 context)**

This table provides calculation expressions for the **design resistances** of **cartridge fired pins** under primarily static actions. It is intended for use in design-by-calculation of mechanical fasteners, using variables that relate to the pin geometry, the connected part(s), and the material strengths. The table is organized into rows/sections that give formulas for different resistance modes and include conditions/inequalities for governing combinations.

**Key symbols referenced in the table (from the surrounding text):**
- \( \gamma_{M2} \): partial factor for mechanical fasteners; recommended value **1.25** (may be given in the National Annex). The table outputs design resistances typically divided by \( \gamma_{M2} \).
- \(A_{net}\): net tensile stress area of the connected part(s).
- \(t_{sup}\): thickness of the supporting member into which the pin is fixed.
- \(d\): nominal pin diameter.
- \(d_w\): diameter of washer or head of the fastener.
- \(f_u\): ultimate tensile strength of the fastener material (used for tension resistance expressions).
- \(F_{v,Rd}\): design shear resistance.
- \(F_{p,Rd}\): design pull-through resistance.
- \(F_{p,Rk}\): corresponding characteristic pull-through resistance (before applying \(\gamma_{M2}\)).
- \(F_{0,Rd}\): design pull-out resistance (often “base metal” failure mode).
- \(F_{t,Rd}\): design tension resistance.
- In several places, the table includes criteria that compare sums of resistances (e.g., \(\sum F_{p,Rd}\), \(\sum F_{v,Rd}\)) with single-fastener resistances multiplied by a factor (e.g., 1.5).

**Shear resistance block (formula-based):**
The table states that the **design shear resistance** \(F_{v,Rd}\) should be taken as:
\[
F_{v,Rd} = F_{v,Rk}/\gamma_{M2}
\]
and explicitly notes that, for this resistance mode, the value is subject to limitations/validity and may require testing in cases marked with a note (shown as \(*3\) in the table). The notation indicates that a characteristic shear capacity \(F_{v,Rk}\) is converted to design value via \(\gamma_{M2}\).

It also provides a **governing condition** involving multiple pins/fasteners, such as:
- **Either** \(\sum F_{b,Rd} \ge 1.5\,F_{n,Rd}\)  
- **Or** \(\sum F_{v,Rd} \ge 1.5\,F_{n,Rd}\)

(As rendered, the table shows an inequality comparing the summed resistance of relevant fasteners to 1.5 times another reference resistance \(F_{n,Rd}\). The intent is to ensure that the connection capacity involving group action is sufficient compared to a controlling single-pin mode.)

**Pull-through / pull-out related block:**
The table gives **pull-through** design resistance \(F_{p,Rd}\) using a thickness-dependent form. A visible expression is:
\[
F_{p,Rd} = \frac{d_w\, t_{fu}}{\gamma_{M2}}
\]
and an alternative reduced expression is shown for a specific action scenario (noted as involving a “combination of wind loads and static loads”), where:
\[
F_{p,Rd} = \frac{0.5\, d_w\, t_{fu}}{\gamma_{M2}}
\]
(So the table encodes different design values depending on the load combination/assessment scenario.)

The table also includes statements that the **governing tensile-type resistance** for the connected parts must satisfy conditions comparing \(\sum F_{p,Rd}\) or \(F_{t,Rd}\) with \(F_{0,Rd}\), expressed as:
\[
\sum F_{p,Rd} \ \ge \ F_{0,Rd}
\quad \text{or} \quad
F_{t,Rd} \ \ge \ F_{0,Rd}
\]
meaning that the designer must verify the relevant fastener resistance is not less than the pull-out/bearing type resistance.

**Tension resistance / geometric validity section:**
The lower portion of the table lists **pin diameter ranges** and associated limits/requirements expressed through ranges involving \(t_{sup}\) (thickness of supporting member). It contains conditional entries such as:
- formulas/coefficients depending on \(d\) intervals (e.g., entries like “\(4.5d\)” appear repeatedly),
- corresponding thickness conditions (e.g., \(3.7\,\text{mm} \le d \le 6.0\,\text{mm}\); and then specific requirements like \(t_{sup} \ge 4.0\,\text{mm}\), or similar threshold pairs for other \(d\) values such as \(d=4.5\,\text{mm}\) with \(t_{sup} > 6.0\,\text{mm}\), etc.).

These rows effectively define the **validity domain** of the tabulated resistance expressions, tying the allowed supporting thickness to the pin diameter (and thus ensuring that failure modes assumed in the derivation are realistic).

**Notes and testing/deformation cautions (from the adjacent text):**
The surrounding clauses linked to tables 8.1–8.4 clarify that:
- mechanical fastener resistances are primarily for predominantly static loads,
- some resistances may need determination **by testing** (noted as \(*3\)),
- and additional reduction factors or deformation-capacity checks may apply under certain connection geometry conditions.

Overall, Table 8.3 is a formula/condition table that gives **design resistances for cartridge fired pins** in different loading modes (shear, pull-through, tension, pull-out checks), consistently expressed through the partial factor \(\gamma_{M2}\) and governed by **geometric/material constraints** on pin diameter \(d\) and supporting thickness \(t_{sup}\).

**Table 8.4: Design resistances for bolts (EN 1993-1-8 context)**

This table provides **design resistance expressions/limits for mechanical fasteners in bolted connections**, specifically **bolts** (Table 8.4). The surrounding text specifies that, for design by calculation under predominantly static loading, resistances must be taken from **EN 1993-1-8 tables 8.1 to 8.4**; for bolts the relevant base values are then checked against connection-level rules (e.g., shear adequacy, pull-through/tension adequacy, and deformation-capacity requirements where needed).

### Key variables and symbols referenced
The table content uses the standard fastener symbols introduced in the accompanying clauses:
- **Fv,Rd**: design resistance in **shear**
- **Ft,Rd**: design resistance in **tension** (pull-through/pull-out framework depending on failure mode)
- **Fp,Rd**: **pull-through resistance** component used in bolt design checks
- **Anet**: net cross-sectional area (of connected part)
- **A**-terms: **A** is gross area of fastener; **As** is tensile stress area; **Anet** is net area of the connected part
- **d**: nominal bolt diameter; **d0**: nominal hole diameter
- **dw**: washer/head diameter
- **e1**: end distance; **e2**: edge distance (with respect to load transfer direction)
- **p2**: bolt spacing perpendicular to load transfer
- **t**: thickness of thinner connected part; **t1** thickness of thicker part; **tsup** supporting member thickness
- **fub**: ultimate tensile strength of bolt material; **fu,sup**: ultimate tensile strength of supporting member
- **βLf**: reduction factor for long joints (EN 1993-1-8, 3.8)
- **γM2**: partial factor for fastener resistances; recommended **γM2 = 1.25**

### Main technical rules visible in the table excerpt
The excerpt indicates several design checks/inequalities:

1. **Upper limit / governing resistance condition for tension-related resistance**
   It shows a form equivalent to ensuring the design tensile/pull-through resistance satisfies:
   - a computed value based on **Anet, fu, and γM2** is **capped** such that  
     **F(n,Rd) ≤ Anet·fu / γM2** (the excerpt shows “Fn,Rd ≤ Anet fu / γM2” conceptually).
   This reflects that the resistance in tension/pull-through is not allowed to exceed the capacity derived from the connected part net area and its strength.

2. **Spacing-based limit involving shear/tension distribution**
   A condition appears relating an **effect** “u” (likely a deformation or spacing-related parameter in the connection check) to:
   - **u ≤ p2**
   This indicates that geometric spacing in the transverse direction constrains the effective engagement/force transfer area used in the design.

3. **Shear capacity verification at connection level**
   A clearly visible inequality is:
   - **ΣFv,Rd ≥ 1.2 F n,Rd**  
   i.e., the sum of design shear resistances from all bolts in the connection must be at least **1.2 times** a relevant normal/tensile force resistance term (**Fn,Rd**).  
   This is a strength interaction rule ensuring sufficient shear transfer to accompany the normal force capacity.

4. **Pull-through resistance limitation and potential test requirement**
   The excerpt includes a note-like statement that **F p,Rd** (pull-through resistance) may need **determination by testing** in certain validity ranges (“to be determined by testing” appears in the table body). It also shows a typical structure where:
   - **Fp,Rd** is expressed using geometry/area terms (e.g., involving **Anet·fu / γM2** or similar),
   - but **only within the applicability limits** of the table; outside them, testing governs.

### Validity/applicability notes captured
The visible bottom section includes applicability constraints such as:
- A **range of validity** depending on resistance determined from tests.
- Typical bolt sizing limitations (e.g., “Minimum bolt size: M6” appears).
- References to using rules up to certain thickness/parameter values (e.g., “t > 0.75 mm” and “t … to 3 mm” are visible), implying thickness governs which formula variant applies.
- A reminder that **National Annex** may add further information (as indicated by the notes around Tables 8.1–8.4 in the provided context).

### Practical interpretation for RAG retrieval
For retrieval, Table 8.4 should be represented as a **set of design-resistance conditions for bolts** with:
- **tension/pull-through resistance derived from connected-part net area and strengths** using **γM2**, sometimes with **caps**,
- **shear adequacy checks** expressed via inequalities involving **ΣFv,Rd** and **Fn,Rd**,
- **geometric spacing limits** (notably **p2**) constraining effective behavior,
- and **validity limitations** requiring **testing** if outside table applicability.

If you want, I can also produce a structured “field list” (JSON-like) of the symbols/inequalities extracted from the snippet for direct use in a vector store schema.

**Table 8.5: Design resistances for spot welds (shear loading)**

Table 8.5 provides the **design resistance values** for a **spot weld group loaded in shear**, and establishes the governing expressions and limits needed to compute the **design shear resistance**, denoted **\(F_{v,Rd}\)**. The table is part of the rules for determining the resistance of spot welds per the referenced design framework, and it is intended to be used after defining the welding process and geometry constraints from the surrounding clauses.

### 1) Resistance basis and symbols
The table is used to determine \(F_{v,Rd}\) from the **weld capacity terms** and the applicable **design partial factor**. In the associated notes (context), the following quantities are central:

- **\(A_{net}\)**: net cross-sectional area of the connected part (in the thinner connected sheet context).
- **\(n_w\)**: number of spot welds in one connection.
- **\(t\)**: thickness of the **thinner** connected part/sheet \([\text{mm}]\).
- **\(t_1\)**: thickness of the **thicker** connected part/sheet (used for compatibility/limits).
- **\(e_1, e_2\)** and **\(p_1, p_2\)**: end/edge distances and spacing parameters, as defined in the referenced section 8.3(5).

For the design partial factor applied to spot-weld design resistances, the table context specifies:
- use **\(\gamma_{M2}\)** (recommended **\(\gamma_{M2}=1.25\)**; may be chosen in the National Annex).

### 2) Governing expressions shown in the table
The excerpted content of Table 8.5 shows that the design resistance is expressed in equivalent forms that relate the resistance of the weld group to either:

- a term based on the **maximum allowable weld resistance** and partial factor, or
- a term based on an **area-based resistance**, reduced by \(\gamma_{M2}\).

Specifically, the table demonstrates the chain of equivalences:

- limiting relationships such as  
  \(F_{b,t,Rd} \le 0.7\, d_s\, f_u / \gamma_{M2}\) and  
  \(F_{b,t,Rd} \le 3.1\, t\, d_s\, f_u / \gamma_{M2}\),
- leading to a consolidated relationship of the form  
  \(F_{b,t,Rd} = 1.4\, t\, e_1\, f_u / \gamma_{M2}\),
- and then further to the equivalent **area form**:  
  \(F_{b,t,Rd} = A_{net}\, f_u / \gamma_{M2}\),
- and finally to a geometric-area expression:  
  \(F_{b,t,Rd} = (\pi/4)\, d_s^2\, f_u / \gamma_{M2}\).

Here **\(f_u\)** denotes the material ultimate strength used in the resistance formulation, and **\(d_s\)** represents an effective spot-weld diameter (or characteristic diameter), whose value is determined from the welding type (fusion vs resistance) in the surrounding clauses.

### 3) Design resistance consistency conditions (minimum/combination)
The table also indicates that the final design resistance for the connection should satisfy **comparisons between alternatives**, expressed as inequalities of the form:

- one condition comparing an individual-weld-based term (e.g., containing \(F_{s,Rd}\), or a weld shear component),
- and another condition comparing a connection-summed term (e.g., \(\Sigma F_{v,Rd}\)),
- both ensuring the design resistance is taken as the **more conservative** (greater required reduction) of the alternatives shown.

The excerpt includes expressions indicating multiplication by **1.25** (i.e., the role of \(\gamma_{M2}\)), reflecting that resistance values are adjusted consistently with the partial factor.

### 4) Geometry/spacings limits included in the table

(1) Unless a second order analysis is carried out, the method given in 10.1.3 and 10.1.4 should be used to allow for the tendency of the free flange to move laterally (thus inducing additional stresses) by treating it as a beam subject to a lateral load qh,Ed, see figure 10.1.
 (2) For use in this method, the rotational spring should be replaced by an equivalent lateral linear spring of stiffness K. In determining K the effects of cross-sectional distortion should also be allowed for. For this purpose, the free flange may be treated as a compression member subject to a non-uniform axial force, with a continuous lateral spring support of stiffness K.
 (3) If the free flange of a purlin is in compression due to in-plane bending (for example, due to uplift loading in a single span purlin), the resistance of the free flange to lateral buckling should also be verified.
 (4) For a more precise calculation, a numerical analysis should be carried out, using values of the rotational spring stiffness CD obtained from 10.1.5.2. Allowance should be made for the effects of an initial bow imperfection of (eo) in the free flange, defined as in 5.3. The initial imperfection should be compatible with the shape of the relevant buckling mode, determined by the eigen-vectors obtained from the elastic first order buckling analysis.
 (5) A numerical analysis using the rotational spring stiffness CD obtained from 10.1.5.2 may also be used if lateral restraint is not supplied or if its effectiveness cannot be proved. When the numerical analysis is carried out, it should take into account the bending in two directions, torsional St Venant stiffness and warping stiffness about the imposed rotation axis.
 (6) If a 2nd order analysis is carried out, effective sections and stiffness, due to local buckling, should be taken into account.

When the numerical analysis is carried out, it should take into account the bending in two directions, torsional St Venant stiffness and warping stiffness about the imposed rotation axis.. (6) If a 2nd order analysis is carried out, effective sections and stiffness, due to local buckling, should be taken into account..
 NOTE: For a simplified design of purlins made of C-, Z- and Σ- cross sections see Annex E.

(1) For gravity loading, a single span purlin should satisfy the criteria for cross-section resistance given in 10.1.4.1. If it is subject to axial compression, it should also satisfy the criteria for stability of the free flange given in 10.1.4.2.
 (2) For uplift loading, a single span purlin should satisfy the criteria for cross-section resistance given in 10.1.4.1 and the criteria for stability of the free flange given in 10.1.4.2.

(1) The moments due to gravity loading in a purlin that is physically continuous over two spans without overlaps or sleeves, may either be obtained by calculation or based on the results of tests.
 (2) If the moments are calculated they should be determined using elastic global analysis. The purlin should satisfy the criteria for cross-section resistance given in 10.1.4.1. For the moment at the internal support, the criteria for stability of the free flange given in 10.1.4.2 should also be satisfied. For mid-support should be checked also for bending moment + support reaction (web crippling if cleats are not used) and for bending moment + shear forces depending on the case under consideration.
 (3) Alternatively the moments may be determined using the results of tests in accordance with Section 9 and Annex A.5 on the moment-rotation behaviour of the purlin over the internal support.
 NOTE: Appropriate testing procedures are given in Annex A.
 (4) The design value of the resistance moment at the supports Msup,Rd for a given value of the load per unit length qEd , should be obtained from the intersection of two curves representing the design values of:
 - the moment-rotation characteristic at the support, obtained by testing in accordance with Section 9 and Annex A.5;
 - the theoretical relationship between the support moment Msup,Ed and the corresponding plastic hinge rotation φEd in the purlin over the support.
 To determine the final design value of the support moment Msup,Ed allowance should be made for the effect of the lateral load in the free flange and/or the buckling stability of that free flange around the mid-support, which are not fully taken into account by the internal support test as given in clause A.5.2. If the free flange is physically continued at the support and if the distance between the support and the nearest anti-sag bar is larger than 0,5 s, the lateral load qh,Ed according to 10.1.4.2 should be taken into account in verification of the resistance at mid-support. Alternatively, full-scale tests for two or multi-span purlins may be used to determine the effect of the lateral load in the free flange and/or the buckling stability of that free flange around the mid- support.

**Table 10.1: Values of initial moment \(M_{0,fz,Ed}\) and correction factor \(\kappa_R\)**

This table provides expressions used to determine the **initial lateral bending moment in the free flange**, \(M_{0,fz,Ed}\), and a corresponding **correction factor** \(\kappa_R\) for different **critical locations along the span** of a purlin (i.e., where the free flange experiences the most adverse lateral bending effects). The table is intended for designs where the purlin free flange lateral bending response is modeled using an idealized **spring support** concept (Winkler foundation approach). It is valid for **spring-support stiffness parameter range \(R \le 40\)**.

### Columns and meaning
The table has three main columns:

1. **Location (m or e)**  
   A location identifier (not fully visible in the crop) that corresponds to specific points along the span, such as:
   - at **supports**,
   - **between anti-sag bars**, and/or
   - **at anti-sag bars** or critical intermediate points.  
   The unit shown is either **\(m\)** (span-related coordinate positions) or **\(e\)** (an offset distance used in the boundary-condition geometry).

2. **\(M_{0,fz,Ed}\)** (units indicated as moment, shown as algebraic expressions)  
   Each row gives the **initial lateral bending moment in the free flange** without accounting for spring-support correction, expressed in terms of:
   - the **equivalent lateral load** \(q_{h,Ed}\),
   - the **distance between anti-sag bars or span** \(L_a\) or related span segment parameter,
   - and a numerical coefficient (e.g., \(1/8\), \(9/128\), \(-1/8\), etc.).  
   The table entries take the general form:
   \[
   M_{0,fz,Ed} = (\text{coefficient}) \, q_{h,Ed}\, L_a^2
   \]
   with sign (positive/negative) reflecting the moment direction at that location.

3. **\(\kappa_R\)** (dimensionless)  
   For each location type, the table provides a rational function of \(R\):
   \[
   \kappa_R = \frac{1 \pm aR}{1 \pm bR}
   \]
   where the coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) differ by location. The factor \(\kappa_R\) is used to correct \(M_{0,fz,Ed}\) for the **effective spring support response** at that location:
   \[
   M_{fz,Ed} = \kappa_R \, M_{0,fz,Ed}
   \]
   (as implied by the adjacent explanatory text in the document).

### Visible row patterns (from the table excerpt)
The excerpt shows five location/moment combinations, each paired with its own \(\kappa_R\):

- \(M_{0,fz,Ed} = \frac{1}{8} q_{h,Ed} L_a^2\), with  
  \(\kappa_R = \dfrac{1 - 0.0225R}{1 + 0.1013R}\)

- \(M_{0,fz,Ed} = \frac{9}{128} q_{h,Ed} L_a^2\), with  
  \(\kappa_R = \dfrac{1 - 0.0141R}{1 + 0.416R}\)

- \(M_{0,fz,Ed} = -\frac{1}{8} q_{h,Ed} L_a^2\), with  
  \(\kappa_R = \dfrac{1 + 0.0314R}{1 + 0.396R}\)

- \(M_{0,fz,Ed} = \frac{1}{24} q_{h,Ed} L_a^2\), with  
  \(\kappa_R = \dfrac{1 - 0.0125R}{1 + 0.198R}\)

- \(M_{0,fz,Ed} = -\frac{1}{12} q_{h,Ed} L_a^2\), with  
  \(\kappa_R = \dfrac{1 + 0.0178R}{1 + 0.191R}\)

### Design interpretation
To apply the table in the stress verification procedure described in the surrounding text, the designer:
1. Computes \(q_{h,Ed}\) (equivalent lateral load acting on the free flange).
2. Identifies the **critical location** along the purlin (matching the row).
3. Reads \(M_{0,fz,Ed}\) for that location as a multiple of \(q_{h,Ed}L_a^2\).
4. Computes \(\kappa_R\) from the row formula using the spring-support parameter \(R\).
5. Obtains the corrected lateral bending moment \(M_{fz,Ed} = \kappa_R M_{0,fz,Ed}\), which then feeds the free-flange stress check (via \(M_{fz,Ed}\) terms in the governing equations).

**“Table 10.2a: Coefficients ηi for down load with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 anti-sag bars.”**

### Purpose and where it is used
In the design checks described in the surrounding text, the table provides **dimensionless coefficients** **η1, η2, η3, and η4** that are required to compute the **relative slenderness** (denoted in the text as **fzλ**) for **flexural buckling of the free flange**. Specifically, equations **(10.8)** and **(10.9)** refer to these coefficients as part of determining buckling resistance for **downward gravity loading** conditions where **anti-sag bars** provide lateral restraint to the free flange.

### Table structure (columns)
The table has one main grouping column indicating:

- **Anti-sag bar number** (0, 1, 2, and “3 and 4”)

and four coefficient columns:

- **η1**
- **η2**
- **η3**
- **η4**

### Table structure (rows / span condition)
The rows are organized by **span condition** (the leftmost text is partially cropped/obscured in the image), but it clearly distinguishes two common beam arrangement categories relevant to buckling calculations:
1. **“Intermediate span”**
2. **“(final/carrying) span”** or “end span” (the wording is partially cut, but the presence of two categories with different coefficient sets implies an end-vs-intermediate span distinction)

Within each span category, the table provides coefficient values for each anti-sag bar count.

### Values shown (as visible)
For each anti-sag bar number, the table lists the following coefficient sets:

#### Anti-sag bars = 0
- **η1 = 0.414**, **η2 = 1.72**, **η3 = 1.11**, **η4 = −0.178** (intermediate span, as shown)
- A second intermediate-span row for this case also appears with **η1 = 0.657**, **η2 = 8.17**, **η3 = 2.22**, **η4 = −0.107** (indicating different span category/row context in the cropped header area)

#### Anti-sag bars = 1

- Another row shows **η1 = 0.596**, **η2 = 2.33**, **η3 = 1.15**, **η4 = −0.192**

#### Anti-sag bars = 2
- One row shows **η1 = 0.596**, **η2 = 2.33**, **η3 = 1.15**, **η4 = −0.192**
- Another row shows **η1 = 0.596**, **η2 = 2.33**, **η3 = 1.15**, **η4 = −0.192** (the image suggests repeated values across adjacent span-condition rows)

#### Anti-sag bars = 3 and 4
- Coefficients shown: **η1 = 0.694**, **η2 = 5.45**, **η3 = 1.27**, **η4 = −0.168**

### Domain of validity (from the provided context)
The surrounding text states that **Tables 10.2a and 10.2b are valid only** for:
- **Equal spans uniformly loaded beam systems**
- **No overlap or sleeve effects** (unless the connection system can be treated as **fully continuous**)
- Anti-sag bars must provide **lateral rigid support** for the **free flange**
- If not in these conditions, buckling length should be obtained using more appropriate calculations, though a conservative simplification may apply (e.g., except cantilevers, using the **3 anti-sag bars per field** case).

### Key takeaway for RAG retrieval
When computing **flexural buckling of the free flange under down load**, retrieve **η1–η4** from **Table 10.2a** using:
- the **number of anti-sag bars** (0, 1, 2, or 3–4),
- the appropriate **span type** (intermediate vs end/other category as indicated by the table’s row grouping),
then substitute these coefficients into the **relative slenderness** expressions referenced by **equations (10.8)–(10.9)**.

**Table 10.2b: Coefficients \( \eta_i \) for uplift load with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 anti-sag bars**

This table provides design coefficients \( \eta_1, \eta_2, \eta_3, \eta_4 \) used in clause (10.9) to determine the relative slenderness \( f_{z\lambda} \) governing **flexural buckling of the free flange** for *uplift loading* situations in purlin/beam systems. The coefficients depend on two parameters:

1. **Number of anti-sag bars (lateral support elements)**
   - Values considered: **0, 1, 2, 3, 4**.
2. **Span location category** within a multi-span or continuous member, reflecting different effective buckling conditions:
   - **End spans** (labelled as “end span”)
   - **Intermediate spans** (labelled as “intermediate span”)
   - **“Intermediate span and end spans”** (explicit combined row groupings in the table)
   - **“3 and 4”** appears as a row group under the span-type grouping, indicating that for certain span locations the coefficients for 3 and 4 anti-sag bars may be identical.

### Table structure and columns
- **First column:** span category (e.g., end span, intermediate span, and end spans combinations).
- **Second column:** anti-sag bar count (column heading: “Anti sag-bar Number”).
- **Next four columns:** coefficient values labeled:
  - \( \eta_1 \)
  - \( \eta_2 \)
  - \( \eta_3 \)
  - \( \eta_4 \)

### Key coefficient trends (from the listed values)
- **Increasing anti-sag bars generally increases \( \eta_2 \) and \( \eta_3 \)**, consistent with increased restraint reducing buckling severity in the coefficient formulation.
- \( \eta_4 \) is **negative in all non-zero anti-sag cases shown** and is **also negative when anti-sag bars are 0** for the relevant span row(s). This suggests \( \eta_4 \) provides a subtractive or correction effect in the uplift buckling expression.
- For a given anti-sag count, **end-span and intermediate-span coefficients differ**, meaning the buckling length/amplification effects vary with boundary conditions along the continuous system.

### Examples of tabulated values
- **0 anti-sag bars:**
  - End span: \( \eta_1 = 0.694,\ \eta_2 = 5.45,\ \eta_3 = 1.27,\ \eta_4 = -0.168\)
  - Intermediate span: \( \eta_1 = 0.515,\ \eta_2 = 1.26,\ \eta_3 = 0.868,\ \eta_4 = -0.242\)

- **2 anti-sag bars:**

  - End spans grouping: \( \eta_1 = 0.902,\ \eta_2 = 8.55,\ \eta_3 = 2.18,\ \eta_4 = -0.111\)
- **3 and 4 anti-sag bars (combined):**

  - Intermediate span: \( \eta_1 = 0.800,\ \eta_2 = 6.75,\ \eta_3 = 1.49,\ \eta_4 = -0.155\)

### How this table is intended to be used in context
Within the broader buckling procedure described in the accompanying text, these \( \eta_i \) values are inserted into the equations for **relative slenderness \( f_{z\lambda} \)** for **uplift loading** when determining buckling resistance of the free flange. The governing equations require selecting the correct coefficient set based on:
- the **number of anti-sag bars**, and
- whether the check applies to an **end span** or **intermediate span** (including the table’s combined span categories).

**Table 10.3: Rotation coefficient \(C_{100}\) for trapezoidal steel sheeting** provides reference values used to compute the rotational spring stiffness \(C_{AD}\) of the purlin–sheeting connection (see Eq. (10.17) in the surrounding text). The table expresses \(C_{100}\) in **kNm/m** as a function of (i) how the sheet is fastened to the purlin (through trough vs through crest), (ii) whether the fasteners are pitched at spacing \(e=b_R\) or \(e=2b_R\) (where \(b_R\) is the sheeting corrugation width), (iii) whether the specified washer/fastener configuration is present, and (iv) the **washer diameter** (in mm). It also reports a corresponding **maximum flange width** \(b_{T,\max}\) (in mm), representing the applicable limit of sheeting flange width through which fastening occurs.

### Column meanings (as shown in the header)
- **Sheet fastened through:** two options  
  - **Trough** (sheet fastened through the trough)  
  - **Crest** (sheet fastened through the crest)
- **Pitch of fasteners:** two options  
  - \(e=b_R\)  
  - \(e=2b_R\)
- **Washer diameter [mm]:** diameter of the saddle washer used with assumed thickness \(t=0.75\) mm (as described in the key/context).
- **\(C_{100}\) [kNm/m]:** tabulated rotation coefficient at the reference condition used in Eq. (10.17). This value is later adjusted using multiplicative factors (e.g., involving \(k_{ba}\), \(k_t\), \(k_{bR}\), \(k_A\), \(k_{bT}\) etc. from the provided context).
- **\(b_{T,\max}\) [mm]:** maximum allowable flange width for which the tabulated \(C_{100}\) remains valid.

### Row structure and selection indicators
Within the body of the table, a **“×” mark** appears in some intermediate columns, indicating the applicable washer/connection configuration for that row. In practice, the user selects the row corresponding to the combination of:
1) **Fastening position** (through trough or through crest),  
2) **Fastener pitch** (\(e=b_R\) or \(e=2b_R\)),  
3) **Washer diameter** (e.g., values appearing include **22**, **16**, etc.), and  
4) The corresponding configuration indicated by the “×” markers.

### Example extracted values
Some visible entries include:
- For **trough fastening** with **washer diameter 22 mm**, \(e=2b_R\): \(C_{100}=5.2\) and \(b_{T,\max}=40\) mm (one row). Another trough/22 mm case gives \(C_{100}=3.1\) with the same \(b_{T,\max}=40\) mm (another marked configuration).
- For **crest fastening** with **washer diameter 22 mm**, \(e=2b_R\): entries show \(C_{100}=3.1\) with \(b_{T,\max}=120\) mm, and also \(C_{100}=2.0\) with \(b_{T,\max}=120\) mm for the marked variant.
- For a **washer diameter 16 mm** (again associated with the trough/crest and pitch selections indicated), entries include \(C_{100}=2.6\) and \(b_{T,\max}=40\) mm, and another marked row with \(C_{100}=1.7\) and \(b_{T,\max}=40\) mm.

### Applicability notes (from the surrounding context)
The table values are stated to be valid only under certain installation/geometric conditions (e.g., limits on sheet-to-purlin screw diameter and constraints related to the “through crest” applicability). These conditions ensure that \(C_{100}\) can be used consistently as the baseline in Eq. (10.17) without extrapolation beyond the tabulated regimes.

Overall, **Table 10.3 is a lookup table** that provides baseline rotation coefficients \(C_{100}\) and allowable maximum fastening flange widths \(b_{T,\max}\) for trapezoidal steel sheeting, depending on **fastening through trough vs crest**, **fastener pitch relative to corrugation**, and **washer diameter/configuration**, to support the determination of the rotational spring stiffness of the purlin–sheeting interface.

**Table 10.4 – Shear force and tensile force in fastener along the beam**

This table provides expressions for the **shear force per unit length** \(q_s\) and the **tensile force per unit length** \(q_t\) acting in a **fastener** that fixes sheeting (or a similar element) to a beam member (described as “along the beam”). The values are presented in terms of design load effects per unit length, component factors, and fastener geometry.

The table is organised with two main columns:

1. **Shear force per unit length \(q_s\)**  
2. **Tensile force per unit length \(q_t\)**  

Each row corresponds to a different loading state/sign combination or arrangement (the leftmost labels are partially cut off in the image, but each row clearly represents a distinct case through the differing formula structure). Across the rows, the formulas follow a pattern using:

- \(E_d\): a reference design load action (appearing multiplied by stiffness or influence terms as shown)
- \(\xi\): a factor modifying how the load is distributed between shear and tension (it repeatedly appears as \(1\pm\xi\) and \(\xi\) alone)
- \(k_h\): an interaction/shape factor (appears in combination with \(\xi\))
- \(h\): a sectional dimension or lever arm height (used in expressions such as \(k_h E_d h\))
- \(a\) and \(b\): geometric or dimensional parameters defining how forces are split; the table includes terms like \((b-a)/h\) indirectly through \((b-a)\) patterns
- The combination \(\frac{h}{a}\), \(\frac{h}{(b-a)}\), and related sums indicate **load sharing between two regions** (likely corresponding to distances to flanges/support points)
- \(l\): another geometric length (appears in the tensile expressions as \(a l + qE_d\) style terms; in the image, it shows as \(h l\) in one place)
- In one row, there is an explicit note that \(a \approx b/2\) for the tensile expression (“\((a \approx b/2)\)” is visible), indicating a simplified case for \(q_t\).

### How to interpret the entries
- **Shear force \(q_s\)** is expressed as either a scaled version of \((1+\xi) k_h E_d\) or \((1-\xi)k_h E_d\), sometimes with a subtraction term involving \(\frac{a}{h}\) (i.e., \(\frac{h-d}{a}\)-type structure but represented here as \(\frac{h-a}{a}\) through the visible terms like \((k_h-a/h)qE_d\)). This indicates that \(q_s\) depends on whether the fastener is carrying mainly shear due to load transfer in one direction or due to tension effects.
- **Tensile force \(q_t\)** is zero in one case, meaning that under that particular loading state the fastener experiences no net tensile force per unit length.
- In other rows, \(q_t\) is proportional to \(\xi k_h E_d\) times a geometric ratio (e.g., \(h/a\) or \(h/(b-a)\)), sometimes **plus or including an additional term** like \(+\,qE_d\) (shown in the image as “\(+ qEd\)”).

### Relation to overall check (context from provided text)
The accompanying text states that for design, fasteners fixing sheeting to purlins should be checked for a **combination of shear force \(q_s e\)** (shear acting perpendicular to the flange) and **tension force \(q_t e\)**, where \(e\) is the fastener pitch. It also clarifies that:
- shear effects from stabilising effects (EN1993-1-1) must be added to shear,
- shear effects due to diaphragm action (parallel to the flange) must be vectorially added to \(q_s\).

Thus, Table 10.4 supplies the *base* \(q_s\) and \(q_t\) distributions along the beam; the final design forces per fastener are then obtained by multiplying by \(e\) and incorporating any additional shear components per the guidance.
